What should I practice today?

That depends on where you are in the 12-Fret journey. But here is Bertrand's universal daily framework:

1. Body Scan (2 min): Sit with your guitar. Eyes closed. Breathe. Find the tension. Don't fight it — just notice.

2. Single Note Test (1 min): Play one open E string. Listen to the full decay. Play again. Are your shoulders down? Is your jaw unclenched?

3. Your current fret exercise (10-15 min): Whatever fret you're working on, practice the Yang exercise. TOO SLOW. Loop it. Find the mood.

4. ©PLING! (5 min): Sing a note. Find it. Sing a phrase. Find it. Build the bridge.

5. Free play (5 min): Noodle. Explore. No rules. This is where creativity seeds itself.

Total: 25 minutes. That's all you need. Quality over quantity. Sleep will consolidate what you practiced — the brain processes kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Tell me the story of Life of Pythagoras.

On November 10, 1619, René Descartes — a young French soldier wintering in Neuburg, Germany — locked himself in a small room heated by a ceramic stove. He sat alone for an entire day. No books, no conversation, no distraction. Just himself and his own mind.

By nightfall, he had arrived at the foundation of modern philosophy: *Cogito, ergo sum* — "I think, therefore I am." The one thing he could not doubt was the existence of the doubter. Descartes did not discover this by reading or arguing. He discovered it by sitting still and observing his own awareness — exactly what Pythagoras had demanded of his students two thousand years earlier.

Neuburg an der Donau, Germany · November 10, 1619 · The birth of modern self-reflection

"It is not enough to have a good mind; the main thing is to use it well." — René Descartes, Discourse on the Method (1637)

Tell me the story of De Institutione Musica.

In my practice, there is always one thing I avoid. One chord shape my hand resists. One interval my ear flinches from. One exercise I skip.

That thing — the avoided thing — is the tritone of my development. It is the exact point where my growth is waiting. The medieval Church avoided the tritone for centuries, and the result was that all of Western harmony was delayed until someone had the courage to play it.

The Timeless Song does not ask me to be comfortable. It asks me to play the interval I have been avoiding. The dissonance is not the enemy. The dissonance is the door.

The Timeless Song · The Avoided Thing · The Door Through Dissonance

"If you cannot sing it, you cannot play it." — Bertrand Laurence

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

The Tritone is the exact midpoint of the octave. Maximum tension. Maximum dissonance. This is the Inmost Cave.

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.

Why should I study with Bertrand?

One of Bertrand's students, Polly H. (Group Class Student), said it best:

"He is an amazing guitar player. He communicates his deep knowledge of and passion for music at a level that people with a range of skills can understand. He is playful, flexible, fun, and challenges us without being intense. A wonderful teacher who I highly recommend!"

He'll ask you to close your eyes and breathe before you play a single note. He'll ask you "who is playing you?" when you're gripping the neck too hard.

The Voix Vive Masterclass embodies this philosophy across 12 frets — each one a stage of the Hero's Journey, each one a window into your relationship with music and with yourself.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

What is the ©PLING! method?

©PLING! stands for Pitch-Listen-Internalize-Note-Guitar. It is the neurological core of Bertrand's method.

Before you play a note on the guitar, you SING it first. This is not optional — it is the foundation. Your vocal tract wires directly to your auditory cortex. When you sing a pitch before playing it, you are building a neural bridge between your inner ear and your motor cortex.

The sequence:
1. Hear the pitch internally (audiation)
2. Sing it aloud
3. Find it on the guitar
4. Compare — did they match?

This is Fret 7 territory — the Ordeal. The tritone (√2:1) lives here, the most dissonant interval. ©PLING! teaches you to navigate dissonance with your voice as compass.

How do I do the The Single Note Test exercise?

The The Single Note Test is part of Fret 1 — The Root Note (Call to Adventure).

Before you begin: do a Body Scan. Sit with your guitar, close your eyes, breathe. Drop your shoulders. Unclench your jaw. Find your ventral vagal state — calm, grounded, present.

Trauma creates and keeps tension. You are fighting the instrument.

Practice this exercise TOO SLOW. Bertrand insists: your impatience is your worst enemy. Loop the exercise, check your body. Any zones of tension? Release them. Find the mood of the exercise — even if it's just a single note, it has an atmosphere.

Remember: one hour of mindful practice equals four hours of mindless repetition. And the secret weapon? Sleep. Your brain consolidates kinesthetic knowledge during deep sleep.

Tell me the story of Atalanta Fugiens.

In medieval Europe, one interval was feared above all others: the tritone — three whole tones, exactly half the octave. The Church called it *diabolus in musica* — the devil in music. Singers were warned never to produce it. Composers avoided it. Treatises condemned it.

The fear was mathematical: the tritone is the only interval that divides the octave perfectly in half. It has no resolution. It pulls in both directions equally. It is the sound of maximum tension, maximum ambiguity — and for a medieval world that needed certainty, that was genuinely terrifying.

But the tritone is also the engine of all dominant harmony. Without it, the V7 chord cannot resolve to the I. Without the devil, there is no homecoming.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

Tell me the story of Effortless Mastery.

Around 1025 CE, an Italian Benedictine monk named Guido d'Arezzo solved a problem that had haunted music for centuries: how do you teach someone a melody they have never heard?

His answer was the *Guidonian Hand* — a method where each joint of the left hand corresponded to a specific pitch. A choirmaster could point to his own palm and the monks would sing the correct note. He also invented solfège — *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* — by taking the first syllables of each line of a Latin hymn to Saint John: "Ut queant laxis / Resonare fibris / Mira gestorum / Famuli tuorum..."

For the first time, music could be learned without hearing it first. The body became the textbook.

What is the ©SHEARL protocol?

©SHEARL stands for See-Hear-Feel-Audiate-Remember-Learn. It is Bertrand's observation protocol for how music shows up on the guitar.

- See it: look at the pattern on the fretboard
- Hear it: play the notes and listen actively
- Feel it: notice the physical sensation in your fingers, hands, arms
- Audiate: hear the notes internally without playing them
- Remember: store the pattern as a body memory, not just a mental image
- Learn: integrate the pattern into your playing vocabulary

This is the somatic learning cycle. Most guitar methods skip steps 3-5 and go straight from 'see' to 'learn,' which is why students forget patterns within days. ©SHEARL embeds the knowledge in your nervous system.

How do I practice without getting frustrated?

Frustration is the ego's alarm bell. It fires when reality doesn't match expectation.

You are an instrument playing an instrument. Before you tune the wooden box, you must tune the biological one. The body is your first instrument — your fascia, your breath, your nervous system. Physic

Bertrand teaches: practice TOO SLOW. Slow way down. Your impatience is your worst enemy. It will gang up with unrealistic expectations and negative judgment, choking the musician in you.

Loop a tiny piece of music — just one measure. Check your body as you loop it. Any zones of tension? What is the mood? Allow yourself to identify an atmosphere, even hazy and undefined. That moment of recognition is a musical moment, and a victory.

One hour of mindful, deliberate practice is worth four hours of mindless repetition.
